brief.topic: The River Adds Its Own Journey

s01: The boat points toward the opposite bank.
Yet its journey drifts to the right.
The river adds a movement of its own.
Imagine a steady current and a boat keeping a constant speed through the water.
Freeze the scene and draw those two movements.
In one second, the boat moves one unit across the water.
The water carries it half a unit downstream.
Put the arrows end to end.
The diagonal joins where the boat started to where it actually arrives.
This is vector addition: both direction and size matter.
To arrive directly opposite, point the boat a little upstream.
Its leftward movement can cancel the river’s rightward movement.
Here the current is half the boat’s speed, so a thirty degree turn is enough.
The remaining movement is straight across.
It is a little slower across than before, because some effort points upstream.
This ideal model ignores changes in current and steering.
Sometimes reaching a place begins by pointing somewhere else.

creative.audience: Curious teens and adults; no specialist prerequisites.
creative.learning_goal: Ground velocity is the vector sum of boat velocity relative to water and water velocity relative to shore.
creative.question: Why does a boat drift away from the direction it points?

creative.novelty_audit: Compared archive titles and authored mechanism index before production. Closest prior: objects/05-walk: harmonic mean of trip speeds. Difference: This is two-dimensional frame-relative vector addition with an upstream cancellation, not averaging outbound and return speeds.. Earlier unavailable transcripts are not fully audited.

profile_application.signature: Recognizable physical subject and useful setting; explicit connection to exact diagram; return to a changed physical condition. Restrained original vector artwork.
profile_application.episode_variation: Keep the boat and banks recognizable, add water-relative and shore-relative displacement arrows, then aim upstream to cancel drift.
exceptions: Exact geometry takes precedence over rounded primitives.
No continuous music bed: proof passages are dry.

scenes.narration:
The boat points toward the opposite bank. Yet its journey drifts to the right. The river adds a movement of its own.

Imagine a steady current and a boat keeping a constant speed through the water. Freeze the scene and draw those two movements. In one second, the boat moves one unit across the water. The water carries it half a unit downstream.

Put the arrows end to end. The diagonal joins where the boat started to where it actually arrives. This is vector addition: both direction and size matter.

To arrive directly opposite, point the boat a little upstream. Its leftward movement can cancel the river’s rightward movement. Here the current is half the boat’s speed, so a thirty degree turn is enough.

The remaining movement is straight across. It is a little slower across than before, because some effort points upstream. This ideal model ignores changes in current and steering. Sometimes reaching a place begins by pointing somewhere else.
